q-pr-collocation.label: Preposition in a fixed phrase
q-pr-collocation.summary: Many nouns and verbs take a particular preposition: under pressure, under conditions, in danger, on duty.

q-pr-gerund.label: Noun + preposition + -ing
q-pr-gerund.summary: After a noun such as reputation, habit, chance, way, the preposition is followed by -ing, not by to + verb.

q-pr-object.label: Verbs that take the person directly
q-pr-object.summary: Ask, tell, request, advise take the person with no preposition: asked the student to submit.

q-pr-amongbetween.label: among vs. between
q-pr-amongbetween.summary: 'Among' treats three or more as one group; 'between' is for exactly two, or for three-plus only when the relationship is one-to-one.

q-pr-timeat.label: Preposition of time
q-pr-timeat.summary: A clock time takes 'at', a month or year takes 'in', a day or date takes 'on' — and today/tomorrow/yesterday/last night take no preposition at all.

q-pr-despite.label: despite vs. in spite of
q-pr-despite.summary: Both mean 'even though', but 'despite' never takes 'of' after it; only 'in spite of' has 'of'.

q-pr-intoin.label: into vs. in (motion vs. position)
q-pr-intoin.summary: 'Into' shows motion ending inside something; 'in' shows a position already inside. 'Enter' and 'throw' both resist 'into'.

rules.text: Learn the preposition with the noun: under conditions / pressure / circumstances, in danger, on duty, at risk. The wrong options are real prepositions that do not belong with the word.
rules.ok: It may occur under prolonged drought conditions.
rules.bad: It may occur towards prolonged drought conditions.

rules.text: After reputation, habit, chance, possibility, way, experience + of, the verb takes -ing: reputation of being honest. 'Reputation to be' is wrong.
rules.ok: She has the reputation of being an honest leader.
rules.bad: She has the reputation to be an honest leader.

rules.text: Verbs such as ask, tell, request, advise, order take the person directly as their object and add 'to' only for the action: asked the student to submit. Do not put 'to' between the verb and the person.
rules.ok: The teacher asked the student to submit the papers.
rules.bad: The teacher asked to the student to submit the papers.

rules.text: 'Among' is for three or more people or things treated together as one group. 'Between' is for exactly two, or for three or more only when each one is linked to each of the others separately (a treaty between three countries). After 'between', use a plural noun or the objective case (between him and me), and never 'each' or 'every' directly.
rules.ok: The prize was shared among the five winners. There is no rivalry between him and me.
rules.bad: The prize was shared between the five winners. There is no rivalry between he and I.

rules.text: A clock time takes 'at' (at 7 o'clock, at noon, at midnight); a month or year takes 'in' (in May, in 2005); a day or date takes 'on' (on Monday, on the 7th). 'Morning' and 'evening' take 'in' alone, but 'on' as well once a specific day or date is attached (on Sunday morning). Today, tomorrow, yesterday, last night and this morning take no preposition at all.
rules.ok: The train arrives at 7 o'clock on Monday in May. We will meet tomorrow.
rules.bad: The train arrives in 7 o'clock on Monday. We will meet on tomorrow.

rules.text: 'In spite of' and 'despite' both mean 'even though' and are followed by a noun or a gerund. Only 'in spite of' carries 'of'; adding 'of' after 'despite' is a common but incorrect slip.
rules.ok: Despite working hard, he failed. In spite of working hard, he failed.
rules.bad: Despite of working hard, he failed.

rules.text: 'Into' marks motion that ends up inside something (jumped into the river); 'in' marks a position already inside (sitting in the classroom). 'Enter' is never followed by 'into' for a place (enter the room, not enter into the room), though the fixed phrase 'enter into an agreement/alliance' keeps it. 'Throw' takes 'in', not 'into'.
rules.ok: He entered the room quietly. He threw the ball in the well.
rules.bad: He entered into the room quietly. He threw the ball into the well.

q-pr-collocation.cue: A blank before a noun phrase (conditions, pressure, circumstances) in a short sentence.
q-pr-collocation.standard: Say the phrase with each option; the one that sounds like a stored phrase is the answer.
q-pr-collocation.fast: Think of the noun's usual company: conditions go with under; pressure goes with under.
q-pr-collocation.eliminate: Cross out prepositions of direction (towards) and of time that do not fit the noun.
traps: Two options may be possible in loose English (amidst); the stored phrase wins.
Between needs two things; it is wrong with a single noun phrase.

q-pr-gerund.cue: A noun like reputation / chance / habit followed by 'to' + verb that you must replace.
q-pr-gerund.standard: Replace 'to be' with 'of being' after the noun. Check the article of the next noun.
q-pr-gerund.fast: Pick the option starting with 'of being' / 'of having' after a noun.
q-pr-gerund.eliminate: Remove options that turn the verb into a noun (to have honesty) or keep to + verb.
traps: 'The honest leader' (with the) changes the meaning to one specific leader.
'To be honesty' mixes a verb and a noun.

q-pr-object.cue: 'asked to the student', 'told to him', 'requested to them' in the given sentence.
q-pr-object.standard: Delete the extra 'to' before the person. Keep 'to' only before the action verb.
q-pr-object.fast: Choose the option with no 'to' between the verb and the person.
q-pr-object.eliminate: Drop options with 'that' + base verb for ask, or with 'told to'.
traps: Using 'to' before the person (asked to the student).
Dropping the article in the object (submit papers vs the papers).

q-pr-amongbetween.cue: Two named things ('between India and Pakistan') or three-plus named things ('among the students') with the preposition blanked out.
q-pr-amongbetween.standard: Count what follows: exactly two things usually means 'between'; three or more treated as one group means 'among'.
q-pr-amongbetween.fast: Two = between. Three or more as a group = among. Three or more but one-to-one = between.
q-pr-amongbetween.eliminate: Drop 'among' whenever only two things are named; drop 'between' before 'each'/'every'.
traps: 'Between him and me' needs the objective case, not 'he and I'.
A treaty or match among three-plus countries can still use 'between' if the link is mutual and pairwise.

q-pr-timeat.cue: A clock time, a month, a year, a day or a date, or words like today/tomorrow/last night, with the preposition blanked out.
q-pr-timeat.standard: Identify what kind of time word follows: clock time -> at, month/year -> in, day/date -> on, today-type word -> none.
q-pr-timeat.fast: At = hour. In = month/year. On = day/date. No preposition before today/tomorrow/yesterday/last night.
q-pr-timeat.eliminate: Drop 'on' before a bare month or year; drop any preposition at all before 'today' or 'tomorrow'.
traps: 'On tomorrow' and 'on last night' wrongly add a preposition that is never used.
'In the morning' takes 'on' as well only once a specific day or date is named.

q-pr-despite.cue: 'Despite' or 'in spite of' near the start of a clause, often with 'of' nearby.
q-pr-despite.standard: Check whether 'of' follows 'despite'; if it does, the sentence is wrong.
q-pr-despite.eliminate: Drop any option that writes 'despite of'.
traps: 'Despite of' is one of the most common single-word insertion errors in spot-the-error questions.

q-pr-intoin.cue: A verb of motion (jump, dive, enter, throw) followed by a blank before a place.
q-pr-intoin.standard: Ask whether the sentence describes movement ending up inside (into) or a position already inside (in); then check if the verb is 'enter' or 'throw', which resist 'into'.
q-pr-intoin.fast: Jump/dive/fall + into (motion). Sit/stay/live + in (position). Enter + no preposition at all (enter the room). Throw + in, not into.
q-pr-intoin.eliminate: Drop 'into' whenever the verb is 'enter' used with a place, or 'throw' with a container.
traps: 'Enter into the room' is wrong; 'enter into an agreement' is the one fixed exception.
'Throw the ball into the well' looks like motion but the fixed idiom uses 'in'.

pyqs.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
Even though the phenomenon is uncommon, it may still occur ___ prolonged drought conditions.
pyqs.why: 'Occur under [certain] conditions' is the standard phrase: events happen under conditions.

a.note: 'Towards' shows direction and does not go with 'conditions'.

b.note: 'Amidst' is understandable, but 'occur under ... conditions' is the stored phrase the test expects.

c.note: 'Between' needs two things; there is one noun phrase here.

pyqs.caution: 'Amidst prolonged drought conditions' is also acceptable in loose English. The key 'under' rests on the stored phrase 'under conditions'.

pyqs.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
She has the reputation [[to be an honest leader]].
pyqs.why: After the noun 'reputation' the preposition 'of' is used, followed by -ing: 'of being an honest leader'.

a.note: 'To have honesty' keeps the wrong 'to' and changes the meaning.

c.note: 'Of being' is right, but 'the honest leader' points to one particular leader; the sentence speaks of being an honest leader in general.

d.note: 'To be honesty' mixes a verb and a noun and keeps the wrong 'to'.

pyqs.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The teacher [[asked to the student to submit the papers]].
options: asked the student that submit the papers
requested the student to submit papers
asked the student to submit the papers
told to the student submit papers
pyqs.why: 'Ask' takes the person directly, with no 'to' before the student, and 'to' only before the action: 'asked the student to submit the papers'.

a.note: 'Ask ... that submit' is not a correct pattern.

b.note: 'Requested the student to submit papers' is grammatical, but it drops 'the' from 'the papers' and changes the verb, so it is not the closest correction.

d.note: 'Told to the student' repeats the extra 'to' and has no 'to' before 'submit'.

pyqs.caution: Option b is grammatical too. The key is the option that makes the smallest change (just delete the extra 'to').

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The workers continued to build the bridge ___ difficult circumstances.

d.note: 'Beside' means next to a thing, not 'in the situation of'.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
He has the habit [[to wake up at five]].
practice.why: After the noun 'habit' use 'of' + -ing: 'of waking up at five'.

c.note: 'For wake' uses a bare verb after a preposition.

d.note: The preposition 'of' is right but the verb must be -ing, not bare.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
There is no chance [[to win the match]] now.
practice.why: After 'no chance' you can use 'of' + -ing: 'of winning the match'. ('A chance to win' is also correct, but it is not among the options.)

b.note: 'For won' uses a past form after a preposition.

d.note: 'That win' misses a subject and the verb is in the wrong form.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The manager [[told to the clerk to send the file]].
options: told the clerk to send the file
said the clerk to send the file
told the clerk send the file
told to send the file the clerk
practice.why: 'Told' takes the person directly, then 'to' before the action.

b.note: 'Said' cannot take 'the clerk' directly as its object.

c.note: The extra 'to' is removed, but the 'to' before 'send' is lost too.

d.note: The action 'send the file' is placed before the person 'the clerk', an order English does not allow after 'told'.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The inheritance was divided ___ the four brothers equally.
practice.why: Four brothers are more than two and are treated as one group, so 'among' is correct.

b.note: 'Between' is reserved for exactly two, or for three-plus only in a one-to-one relationship; a simple equal division among four people is 'among'.

c.note: 'Amidst' fits an uncountable or abstract surrounding, not a literal division of shares.

d.note: 'Across' shows spread over a surface or area, not a division of shares.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
There is no / secret between / you and I / about this plan.
practice.why: After 'between', the objective case is required, so it should be 'you and me', not 'you and I'.

a.note: 'There is no' is a correct opening.

b.note: 'Secret between' correctly sets up a relationship between exactly two people.

d.note: 'About this plan' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The ceremony will begin ___ 9 o'clock ___ the morning of the 15th.
practice.why: A clock time takes 'at' (at 9 o'clock); once a specific date is attached to 'morning', it takes 'on' (on the morning of the 15th).

b.note: This swaps 'at' and 'in'; a clock time never takes 'in'.

d.note: 'In the morning of the 15th' drops the 'on' that a specific date adds back.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
She promised to / call me back / on tomorrow / before noon.
practice.why: 'Tomorrow' never takes a preposition; the correct phrase is simply 'tomorrow before noon'.

a.note: 'She promised to' is a correct opening.

b.note: 'Call me back' is a correct continuation.

d.note: 'Before noon' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The constitution of India came into force ___ 1950.
practice.why: A bare year takes 'in', not 'on' or 'at'.

b.note: 'On' is for a day or date, not a bare year.

c.note: 'At' is for a clock time, not a year.

d.note: 'Since' marks a starting point used with a perfect tense, not a plain past fact like this.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
[[Despite of]] his old age, he still runs five kilometres daily.
practice.why: 'Despite' never takes 'of'; it is used on its own directly before the noun or gerund.

b.note: 'In spite' on its own, without 'of', is incomplete; the full phrase needs 'in spite of'.

c.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

d.note: 'Although' is a conjunction joining two clauses and is never followed by 'of' or used before a bare noun phrase like this.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
___ repeated warnings, the workers did not stop the unsafe practice.
practice.why: 'In spite of' is the correct form with 'of'; 'despite' would drop the 'of' instead.

b.note: 'Despite of' wrongly adds 'of' after 'despite', which never takes it.

c.note: 'Although' is a conjunction and cannot be followed directly by 'of' and a noun phrase.

d.note: 'However' does not fit this slot grammatically; it does not introduce a noun phrase this way.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The old man / entered into the / room without / knocking on the door.
practice.why: 'Enter' is never followed by 'into' when the object is a place; it should read 'entered the room'.

a.note: 'The old man' is a correct opening subject.

c.note: 'Room without' is a correct continuation once 'into' is dropped.

d.note: 'Knocking on the door' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The frightened boy threw the stolen watch ___ the well and ran away.
practice.why: The fixed idiom with 'throw' takes 'in', not 'into', even though the action is one of motion.

b.note: 'Into' looks like the natural choice for motion, but the idiom with 'throw' fixes 'in' instead.

c.note: 'On' does not fit the sense of dropping something inside a well.

d.note: 'At' would mean aiming towards the well, not dropping something inside it.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
After months of talks, the two companies finally [[entered an agreement]] to share technology.
practice.why: 'Enter into an agreement/alliance' is the one fixed exception where 'enter' does take 'into'.

b.note: 'Entered in an agreement' uses the wrong preposition for this fixed exception.

c.note: 'Entered to an agreement' is not a recognised form of the phrase.

d.note: This repeats the original sentence, which is missing the 'into' this fixed phrase requires.
